title: Flat Features, Detailed Images? Simple Detail Control for Diffusion Transformers

paper.title:
Flat Features, Detailed Images?
Simple Detail Control for Diffusion Transformers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Prompt engineering is commonly used to encourage text-to-image models to generate more detailed images.
However, it does not provide reliable, continuous, or disentangled control.
We analyze feature tokens produced with and without detail-enhancing prompts across six diffusion transformers and observe a common pattern: these prompts tend to
increase the entropy of each token’s energy distribution
while largely preserving its ordering.
That is, flattening the distribution increases the level of detail.
Motivated by this counter-intuitive finding, we introduce a simple training-free approach that continuously adjusts the level of detail according to a scalar.
Specifically, it shifts the squared channel magnitudes of each token toward a higher entropy distribution with a time-aware scheduler to concentrate the intervention at intermediate sampling steps.
Across extensive experiments on different types of diffusion transformers, we show that our approach provides continuous control over detail metrics while largely preserving image quality and semantic structure.
It requires only a few lines of code and adds negligible inference time overhead.
Code is available at TerrysLearning/TokenFlat .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Prompt engineering is a straightforward approach that can be used to enhance visual detail in images generated by text-to-image (T2I) models ( Liu & Chilton, 2022 ; Mo et al., 2024 ) , for example, by adding phrases such as “highly detailed” or “fine texture”. However, such instructions provide vague control, making their strength difficult to specify precisely. Their effects are also unpredictable and model-dependent, as different models may interpret the same phrase differently. Moreover, prompt-based control is not localized and may alter the global semantic structure, complicating iterative refinement. We aim to understand how such detail-focused prompt engineering impacts feature tokens internally, and whether universal patterns exist that can be leveraged for finer control. Flow-matching models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) with diffusion transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) have emerged as a dominant paradigm for T2I generation. We first investigate how such prompts affect feature tokens in pretrained DiTs. Given the same image embedding, we compare the features obtained with and without detail instructions in the prompt. Across six variants of DiTs, we analyze all tokens at every layer and inference timestep. We find that detail-based instructions consistently increase the entropy of the token’s energy distribution, that is, the distribution of its squared channel amplitudes, while largely preserving their rank ordering. In contrast, adding content descriptions rather than detail descriptions exhibits this pattern weakly or not at all. This observation suggests that detail richness could be controlled in a training-free manner by directly rescaling channel magnitudes. It may seem counter-intuitive that flattening a token’s feature distribution should make the associated image patch less flat. We speculate that activating a sparse set of feature dimensions encodes a specific texture, so activating a larger set (i.e., a higher entropy distribution) leads to a mixture of textures. Motivated by this finding, we introduce T ♭ \flat (Token Flattening), a simple mechanism for controlling the level of detail in the generated images according to a user-specified scalar α \alpha . T ♭ \flat linearly interpolates the per-token distribution of squared channel amplitudes (i.e., its energy distribution) with the uniform distribution, increasing its entropy. To improve stability, we design a time-aware scheduler that emphasizes the intervention at intermediate sampling stages. T ♭ \flat requires only a few lines of code and can be applied directly to DiTs as a plug-in. We evaluate T ♭ \flat on three representative diffusion transformers: FLUX.2 Klein 9B, FLUX.2 Klein 9B Base, and Qwen-Image ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , covering distilled and undistilled variants with both single and double stream architectures. Varying α \alpha produces continuous changes across all evaluated detail metrics while largely preserving text alignment, perceptual quality, and semantic structure. Some qualitative examples are demonstrated in fig. 1 . Compared with existing training-free detail-enhancement methods, T ♭ \flat achieves greater structure-preserving detail improvements and increased image quality, with negligible additional inference time overhead.

sections.heading: Diffusion transformers.
sections.text: Previously, diffusion models were based on U-Net architectures ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Nowadays, Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) are dominant due to their better performance and scalability. Text-conditioned DiTs have evolved into several architectural variants. For example, text embeddings can be incorporated into the image stream via cross-attention ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . In MMDiT architectures, text and image embeddings are processed in two separate streams, with joint attention enabling interaction between the two modalities ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . In single-stream architectures, text and image embeddings are concatenated into a unified sequence and processed jointly through self-attention ( Team et al., 2025 ) . Some models combine both designs, using dual-stream blocks followed by single-stream blocks ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) . Furthermore, some alternatives leverage linear attention instead to speed up inference ( Xie et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Manipulating T2I models at inference time.
sections.text: Given a pretrained text-to-image model, its inference process can be manipulated to achieve various desired effects. For example, some methods scale up test-time computation through search or optimization to obtain more desirable generations according to a preference model ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025a ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . Other methods improve generation quality and mitigate sampling artifacts by constructing degraded internal predictions as negative references ( Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Hong, 2024 ) . Ma et al. (2026) ; Bu et al. (2025) enable models to generate images beyond their training resolution. Prior work has also adapted T2I models for image editing ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) , inpainting ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , super-resolution ( Saharia et al., 2023 ) , interpolation ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , 3D generation ( Poole et al., 2023 ) , and personalized generation ( Ruiz et al., 2023 ) . Our work aims to provide a knob for controlling the detail level of generated images. Some closely related methods enhance the detail of images by amplifying high-frequency energy, including FreeU ( Si et al., 2024 ) , Fresca ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , and FDG ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) . However, FreeU is designed for U-Nets, while Fresca and FDG target undistilled models that use CFG ( Ho & Salimans, 2021 ) . Furthermore, Gan et al. (2026) enhances detail through negative guidance constructed by masking the massively activated channels, but requires an additional model forward pass, which causes large extra inference computation. Chen et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) do this through prompt manipulation but do not provide continuous control. In contrast, our method generalizes across DiT architectures while being efficient and explicitly controllable.

sections.heading: Detail instructions largely preserve the rank of channel magnitudes.
sections.text: For each pair of corresponding tokens, we measure the Spearman correlation between their channel-magnitude ranks and average it over all token pairs. Under detail instructions, the correlation ranges from 0.878 to 0.966 across models, where 1.0 indicates perfect rank preservation and 0.0 indicates no correlation. This result suggests that detail instructions tend not to alter the relative importance of different channels, which provides a useful cue to allow a simple training-free control.

sections.heading: These findings are specific to detail instructions.
sections.text: Does this effect arise simply from longer prompts or specifically from detail-oriented instructions? To distinguish these factors, we add a content-adding baseline generated by an LLM that appends additional semantic information to the original prompt, such as adjectives and overall style descriptions. Under additional content, neither the entropy change nor the agreement ratio shows a consistent trend. Its Spearman correlation is also lower than that of detail conditioning, suggesting that extra semantic content changes the channel scale ordering more strongly. Thus, longer prompts alone do not explain the consistent effects of adding detail instructions. sections.heading: 4 Simple Detail Control in Diffusion Transformers
sections.text: To mimic the above observed patterns, we propose a simple training-free mechanism named T ♭ \flat that allows users to explicitly control the detail richness of generated images through a scalar parameter α \alpha on DiTs. The overall procedure is outlined in fig. 3 .

At early steps, our method tends to enhance low-frequency details, such as adding objects; but it may also alter the global semantic structure if applying it too early. At later steps, T ♭ \flat introduces more localized, high-frequency details, such as subtle freckles on faces and coarse fabric textures. That motivates our time-aware scheduler design in section 4 . We model the interpolation strength λ \lambda in eq. 4 by scaling α \alpha according to the current σ t \sigma_{t} . A flow-matching or diffusion model progressively samples from a standard Gaussian distribution ( σ t = 1 \sigma_{t}=1 ), toward a high-density data point ( σ t = 0 \sigma_{t}=0 ). We observe that applying our operation at early timesteps alters more low-frequency components, which may undesirably affect the global semantic structure. At late timesteps, it mainly alters high-frequency components, causing very localized changes. A qualitative example is shown in fig. 4 . We therefore aim to concentrate the guidance on intermediate timesteps, where it primarily affects mid-frequency components that correspond to meaningful details. sections.heading: 5 Experiment
sections.text: In this section, we first demonstrate the performance of T ♭ \flat on three DiTs in section 5.1 . Then, we compare T ♭ \flat with other related methods in section 5.2 . Finally, we provide further discussion of the choice of density formulation, the time-wise effect, and the limitations in section 5.3 .

sections.heading: Models and implementation details
sections.text: We use three representative diffusion transformers: FLUX.2 Klein 9B Base, its distilled variant FLUX.2 Klein 9B ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) , and Qwen-Image (20B) ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . The Base and Qwen models use 25 inference steps with a classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 4, whereas the distilled model uses 4 steps without CFG. All models generate 768 × 768 768\times 768 images. For the time-aware scheduler, we set κ = 40 \kappa=40 for all models and ρ = 0.9 \rho=0.9 , 0.7 0.7 , and 0.8 0.8 for the distilled, Base, and Qwen models. More details are provided in section B.2 .

sections.heading: Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: To assess image quality, we use CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) (Long-CLIP-L, ViT-L/14) and HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025b ) (based on Qwen2-VL-7B) to evaluate text-image alignment and human preference. We quantify image detail using four metrics: edge strength (mean gradient magnitude), sharpness (Laplacian variance), spectral edge frequency f 95 f_{95} (radial frequency enclosing 95% of Hann-windowed Fourier energy, in cycles per pixel), and wavelet detail energy ( Mallat, 1989 ) . Detailed definitions of them are provided in section B.7 . Higher values across these metrics indicate stronger detail components. We assess structure preservation by comparing generated images and the baseline, using DINO ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) cosine distance between the CLS tokens and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) computed after downsampling both images to 128 × 128 128\times 128 .

More examples in section B.9 . Several existing training-free methods may also enhance image details. First, we compare against methods that introduce additional guidance, including SAG ( Hong et al., 2023 ) , PAG ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) , SEG ( Hong, 2024 ) , TPG ( Rajabi et al., 2025 ) , DG ( Gan et al., 2026 ) , and SSG ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These methods employ CFG-like operations to steer the sampling process away from negative predictions constructed by perturbing intermediate features in different ways. We also compare with FreSca ( Huang et al., 2025 ) and FDG ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) , which apply different guidance weights to the high and low frequency components of the CFG term. Finally, we compare with HiGS ( Sadat et al., 2026 ) , which enhances details using a weighted average of historical predictions. For a fair comparison, we apply all methods to FLUX.2 Klein 9B Base using identical settings and the same prompt set. We progressively increase the guidance strength of each method until its structural deviation from the baseline exceeds that of ours. Even at this point, our T ♭ \flat achieves higher detail metrics. This indicates that our method provides more effective, detail-focused control. In terms of image quality, while all the methods maintain a similar level of CLIP score, T ♭ \flat delivers the highest HPSv3 preference. In addition, most guidance methods require about 0.5 × 0.5\times more inference computation, while T ♭ \flat only adds a negligible overhead of 3 % 3\% . We report the results and the added computation over baseline in table 3 . A qualitative comparison is shown in fig. 6 .

sections.heading: Time-aware effects of T ♭ \bm{\flat} .
sections.text: We apply T ♭ \flat at one sampling step at a time with a fixed guidance weight α > 0 \alpha>0 using the four-step FLUX.2 Klein 9B model. In fig. 7 , we report the percentage change in spectral energy across five frequency bands, whose definitions are provided in section B.4 . Early interventions distribute the energy change relatively evenly across frequencies, whereas later interventions increasingly amplify high-frequency energy. Figure 8 shows that early interventions cause larger structural deviations from the baseline. A qualitative example is provided in fig. 4 . Together, these observations motivate the time-aware scheduler in section 4 , which emphasizes guidance at intermediate sampling steps. Figure 9 visualizes the scheduler curves: ρ \rho determines the peak location, while κ \kappa controls the width. A larger κ \kappa produces a sharper and more concentrated schedule. Both parameters can be adjusted to accommodate different user preferences.

sections.heading: Why not define density using absolute magnitudes?
sections.text: In eq. 1 , we define channel density using squared magnitudes. A straightforward alternative is to use absolute magnitudes. We repeat the analysis in fig. 2 with this definition and report the results in table 4 . Compared with squared magnitudes, absolute ones yield lower entropy-increase ratios. We attribute this difference to the amplification effect of squaring. Squaring emphasizes changes among higher-magnitude channels while suppressing contributions from lower ones. This reveals that detail instructions redistribute density primarily among highly active channels. This observation is consistent with prior findings on massive activations, where tokens are often sparse and dominated by few channels ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Gan et al., 2025 ; Yehezkel et al., 2026 ) . The effect is more pronounced for models with sparser tokens.

sections.heading: T ♭ \bm{\flat} relies on the model capabilities.
sections.text: We further evaluate T ♭ \flat on the other DiT families. As reported in table 7 , T ♭ \flat retains monotonic control over most detail metrics but is less effective than on stronger FLUX and Qwen models, and image quality and structural similarity decline faster for the same change. We hypothesize that stronger models learn a more densely populated feature space and tolerate token perturbations better, whereas perturbing weaker models may more easily push features outside the learned distribution, degrading image quality. This dependence on the inherent capability of the pretrained model represents a limitation of T ♭ \flat as a training-free method.

sections.heading: Failure cases and future work.
sections.text: T ♭ \flat operates within a limited effective range and may come with some side effects. Additional examples are provided in section B.8 . A fixed pushing toward a uniform target is unlikely to be the optimal direction for every token, but characterizing a per-token optimal direction is hard for a training-free method. We hope this observation motivates future work that enables fine-grained control over detail, which is further discussed in appendix C .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We analyze how detail-guided prompts alter feature tokens across diffusion transformers and identify a consistent pattern. Motivated by this observation, we propose T ♭ \flat , a simple training-free method for controlling detail richness with a user-specified scalar. Our work provides insight into the mechanisms behind prompt engineering and an effective method for precise detail control.

sections.heading: A.1 Detail instruction search
sections.text: Before the analysis in section 3 , we search for a model-specific prompt suffix that consistently elicits more visual details from each model. Specifically, we first did a detail-guided prompt search for each model to get phrases that can enable more detail, measured by the Fourier high-frequency energy ratio. We build a phrase bank from an LLM: e.g. “ultra detailed”, “fine textures”, “micro-contrast”, and selected phrases as a suffix for each prompt and did a voting based on the increase of the detail measurement. Each model gets the highest-voted phrases to use as a suffix. In the end, we get the phrases for each model and use them as suffix. Then we input the same image VAE latent to the diffusion transformer with different text conditions, one with the original prompt and the other with the detail-guided suffixes. After the search, we use the following model-specific suffixes in the final analysis experiments: “hyper realistic, ultra detailed, high resolution” for FLUX.2, “intricate surface detail, fine textures, ultra detailed” for SD3.5, and “micro-contrast, studio lighting, fine textures” for Z-Image. During this prompt search, we also have some interesting findings. Effective detail-guided suffixes are strongly model-dependent. For example, “ultra detailed” increases the FFT-based detail score for FLUX.2 but decreases it for Z-Image. Across our search, the preferred suffixes vary more across models than across input prompts, indicating that detail instructions are more model-dependent than prompt-dependent. Longer suffixes provide no consistent benefit and can even reduce detail; empirically, two to four phrases are sufficient. It suggests that prompt engineering is not a very reliable way to control details, and T ♭ \flat provides a more robust alternative.

sections.heading: B.3 More about the competing method DG
sections.text: Our findings share some similarities with DG ( Gan et al., 2026 ) : both study token-channel magnitudes, and both relate to image detail. We clarify the differences below. Mechanistically, the two guidance signals differ: DG requires an extra forward pass to construct its negative-guidance prediction, while T ♭ \flat does not. This is reflected in table 3 , where DG costs 1.53 × 1.53\times the baseline latency versus 1.03 × 1.03\times for T ♭ \flat . The underlying findings also differ. DG observes massive activations: a few channels dominate a token, and masking them out causes only local distortion rather than structural change. DG therefore uses the masked prediction as negative guidance. This is effective at fixing local corruptions such as blur or unclear detail. Their method primarily serves as a safeguard against local detail degradation rather than a mechanism for further enhancing already well-rendered details. In contrast, we compare model behavior with and without a detail instruction and use that difference to construct a direction that increases detail continuously.

sections.text: Table 1 also shows that entropy does not increase for every token: the agreement ratio A all A_{\mathrm{all}} stays well below 100% for all models. This suggests that each token likely has its own optimal direction for detail enhancement, rather than sharing a single one. T ♭ \flat instead pushes every token’s channel density toward a more uniform distribution, which is unlikely to be optimal for every token. However, characterizing a per-token optimal direction is difficult for a training-free method. We hope this observation motivates future work on training a network that enables fine-grained, per-token control over detail.

Simple Detail Control for Diffusion Transformers Qingtao Yu Zhen Wang Jiyang Zheng Minghao Sun Hongdong Li Dylan Campbell The Australian National University Microsoft The University of Queensland {terry.yu,zhen.wang,minghao.sun,hongdong.li,dylan.campbell}@anu.edu.au, jiyang.zheng@microsoft.com Abstract Prompt engineering is commonly used to encourage text-to-image models to generate more detailed images. However, it does not provide reliable, continuous, or disentangled control. We analyze feature tokens produced with and without detail-enhancing prompts across six diffusion transformers and observe a common pattern: these prompts tend to increase the entropy of each token’s energy distribution while largely preserving its ordering. That is, flattening the distribution increases the level of detail. Motivated by this counter-intuitive finding, we introduce a simple training-free approach that continuously adjusts the level of detail according to a scalar. Specifically, it shifts the squared channel magnitudes of each token toward a higher entropy distribution with a time-aware scheduler to concentrate the intervention at intermediate sampling steps. Across extensive experiments on different types of diffusion transformers, we show that our approach provides continuous control over detail metrics while largely preserving image quality and semantic structure. It requires only a few lines of code and adds negligible inference time overhead. Code is available at TerrysLearning/TokenFlat . α ↓ \alpha\downarrow Detail ↓ \downarrow α = 0 \alpha=0 Baseline α ↑ \alpha\uparrow Detail ↑ \uparrow Qwen Image A cool girl with pink pigtails, face tattoos and the word “simple” tattooed across her collarbone FLUX.2 klein 9B A cute dog in front of a glowing Christmas tree, holding a toy house painted with the word “Effective” Figure 1: Qualitative examples of our method across two representative diffusion transformers. Our method controls detail richness through a user-specified scalar α \alpha as a lightweight plugin. 1 Introduction Prompt engineering is a straightforward approach that can be used to enhance visual detail in images generated by text-to-image (T2I) models ( Liu & Chilton, 2022 ; Mo et al., 2024 ) , for example, by adding phrases such as “highly detailed” or “fine texture”. However, such instructions provide vague control, making their strength difficult to specify precisely. Their effects are also unpredictable and model-dependent, as different models may interpret the same phrase differently. Moreover, prompt-based control is not localized and may alter the global semantic structure, complicating iterative refinement. We aim to understand how such detail-focused prompt engineering impacts feature tokens internally, and whether universal patterns exist that can be leveraged for finer control. Flow-matching models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) with diffusion transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) have emerged as a dominant paradigm for T2I generation. We first investigate how such prompts affect feature tokens in pretrained DiTs. Given the same image embedding, we compare the features obtained with and without detail instructions in the prompt. Across six variants of DiTs, we analyze all tokens at every layer and inference timestep. We find that detail-based instructions consistently increase the entropy of the token’s energy distribution, that is, the distribution of its squared channel amplitudes, while largely preserving their rank ordering. In contrast, adding content descriptions rather than detail descriptions exhibits this pattern weakly or not at all. This observation suggests that detail richness could be controlled in a training-free manner by directly rescaling channel magnitudes. It may seem counter-intuitive that flattening a token’s feature distribution should make the associated image patch less flat. We speculate that activating a sparse set of feature dimensions encodes a specific texture, so activating a larger set (i.e., a higher entropy distribution) leads to a mixture of textures. Motivated by this finding, we introduce T ♭ \flat (Token Flattening), a simple mechanism for controlling the level of detail in the generated images according to a user-specified scalar α \alpha . T ♭ \flat linearly interpolates the per-token distribution of squared channel amplitudes (i.e., its energy distribution) with the uniform distribution, increasing its entropy. To improve stability, we design a time-aware scheduler that emphasizes the intervention at intermediate sampling stages. T ♭ \flat requires only a few lines of code and can be applied directly to DiTs as a plug-in. We evaluate T ♭ \flat on three representative diffusion transformers: FLUX.2 Klein 9B, FLUX.2 Klein 9B Base, and Qwen-Image ( Black Forest Labs, 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , covering distilled and undistilled variants with both single and double stream architectures. Varying α \alpha produces continuous changes across all evaluated detail metrics while largely preserving text alignment, perceptual quality, and semantic structure. Some qualitative examples are demonstrated in fig. 1 . Compared with existing training-free detail-enhancement methods, T ♭ \flat achieves greater structure-preserving detail improvements and increased image quality, with negligible additional inference time overhead. 2 Related Work Diffusion transformers. Previously, diffusion models were based on U-Net architectures ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Nowadays, Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) are dominant due to their better performance and scalability. Text-conditioned DiTs have evolved into several architectural variants. For example, text embeddings can be incorporated into the image stream via cross-attention ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . In MMDiT architectures, text and image embeddings are processed in two separate streams, with joint attention enabling interaction between the two modalities ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . In single-stream architectures, text and image embeddings are concatenated into a unified sequence and processed jointly through self-attention ( Team et al., 2025 ) . Some models combine both designs, using dual-stream blocks followed by single-stream blocks ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2026 ) . Furthermore, some alternatives leverage linear attention instead to speed up inference ( Xie et al., 2025 ) . Manipulating T2I models at inference time. Given a pretrained text-to-image model, its inference process can be manipulated to achieve various desired effects. For example, some methods scale up test-time computation through search or optimization to obtain more desirable generations according to a preference model ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025a ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) . Other methods improve generation quality and mitigate sampling artifacts by constructing degraded internal predictions as negative references ( Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Hong, 2024 ) . Ma et al. (2026) ; Bu et al. (2025) enable models to generate images beyond their training resolution. Prior work has also adapted T2I models for image editing ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) , inpainting ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) , super-resolution ( Saharia et al., 2023 ) , interpolation ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , 3D generation ( Poole et al., 2023 ) , and personalized generation ( Ruiz et al., 2023 ) . Our work aims to provide a knob for controlling the detail level of generated images. Some closely related methods enhance the detail of images by amplifying high-frequency energy, including FreeU ( Si et al., 2024 ) , Fresca ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , and FDG ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) . However, FreeU is designed for U-Nets, while Fresca and FDG target undistilled models that use CFG ( Ho & Salimans, 2021 ) . Furthermore, Gan et al. (2026) enhances detail through negative guidance constructed by masking the massively activated channels, but requires an additional model forward pass, which causes large extra inference computation. Chen et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) do this through prompt manipulation but do not provide continuous control. In contrast, our method generalizes across DiT architectures while being efficient and explicitly controllable. 3 The Effect of Detail-Enhancing Prompts Image Latent (VAE Space) DiT Block DiT Block “A dog.” “A dog. Detail instructions largely preserve the rank of channel magnitudes. For each pair of corresponding tokens, we measure the Spearman correlation between their channel-magnitude ranks and average it over all token pairs. Under detail instructions, the correlation ranges from 0.878 to 0.966 across models, where 1.0 indicates perfect rank preservation and 0.0 indicates no correlation. This result suggests that detail instructions tend not to alter the relative importance of different channels, which provides a useful cue to allow a simple training-free control. These findings are specific to detail instructions. Does this effect arise simply from longer prompts or specifically from detail-oriented instructions? To distinguish these factors, we add a content-adding baseline generated by an LLM that appends additional semantic information to the original prompt, such as adjectives and overall style descriptions. Under additional content, neither the entropy change nor the agreement ratio shows a consistent trend. Its Spearman correlation is also lower than that of detail conditioning, suggesting that extra semantic content changes the channel scale ordering more strongly. Thus, longer prompts alone do not explain the consistent effects of adding detail instructions. Figure 8 shows that early interventions cause larger structural deviations from the baseline. A qualitative example is provided in fig. 4 . Together, these observations motivate the time-aware scheduler in section 4 , which emphasizes guidance at intermediate sampling steps. Figure 9 visualizes the scheduler curves: ρ \rho determines the peak location, while κ \kappa controls the width. A larger κ \kappa produces a sharper and more concentrated schedule. Both parameters can be adjusted to accommodate different user preferences. Why not define density using absolute magnitudes? In eq. 1 , we define channel density using squared magnitudes. A straightforward alternative is to use absolute magnitudes. We repeat the analysis in fig. 2 with this definition and report the results in table 4 . Compared with squared magnitudes, absolute ones yield lower entropy-increase ratios. We attribute this difference to the amplification effect of squaring. Squaring emphasizes changes among higher-magnitude channels while suppressing contributions from lower ones. This reveals that detail instructions redistribute density primarily among highly active channels. This observation is consistent with prior findings on massive activations, where tokens are often sparse and dominated by few channels ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Gan et al., 2025 ; Yehezkel et al., 2026 ) . The effect is more pronounced for models with sparser tokens. T ♭ \bm{\flat} relies on the model capabilities. We further evaluate T ♭ \flat on the other DiT families. As reported in table 7 , T ♭ \flat retains monotonic control over most detail metrics but is less effective than on stronger FLUX and Qwen models, and image quality and structural similarity decline faster for the same change. We hypothesize that stronger models learn a more densely populated feature space and tolerate token perturbations better, whereas perturbing weaker models may more easily push features outside the learned distribution, degrading image quality. This dependence on the inherent capability of the pretrained model represents a limitation of T ♭ \flat as a training-free method. Failure cases and future work. T ♭ \flat operates within a limited effective range and may come with some side effects. Additional examples are provided in section B.8 . A fixed pushing toward a uniform target is unlikely to be the optimal direction for every token, but characterizing a per-token optimal direction is hard for a training-free method. We hope this observation motivates future work that enables fine-grained control over detail, which is further discussed in appendix C . 6 Conclusion We analyze how detail-guided prompts alter feature tokens across diffusion transformers and identify a consistent pattern. Motivated by this observation, we propose T ♭ \flat , a simple training-free method for controlling detail richness with a user-specified scalar.
